prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: Checkout A/B Test Results (language en).
Grid: 7 columns × 9 rows. Row headers: yes (first logical column identifies each row).
Merged cells: "Metric" spans 1 col × 2 row; "Control" spans 2 col × 1 row; "Variant" spans 2 col × 1 row; "Lift" spans 1 col × 2 row; "p-value" spans 1 col × 2 row.
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Metric" · longest unbreakable word 100px · one-line width 263px
  col 2: header "Control › Mean" · longest unbreakable word 50px · one-line width 52px
  col 3: header "Control › 95% CI" · longest unbreakable word 58px · one-line width 113px
  col 4: header "Variant › Mean" · longest unbreakable word 49px · one-line width 50px
  col 5: header "Variant › 95% CI" · longest unbreakable word 58px · one-line width 110px
  col 6: header "Lift" · longest unbreakable word 52px · one-line width 52px
  col 7: header "p-value" · longest unbreakable word 47px · one-line width 55px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 360px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 359px.
This table cannot fit without splitting words at 360px. You MAY choose a total wider than 359px (the reader then scrolls horizontally), or squeeze and accept splits — a design decision.
Rendering convention: the screenshot always shows the WHOLE table. Anything beyond the dashed box is not clipped; it is the part a reader reaches by scrolling sideways, so judge both what fits in the box at first sight and the cost of scrolling to the rest.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

The image shows the table's content with every cell on one line, so you can read everything. Study it first.
1) Understand it: what is the table for, how will people read, scan and compare it, which columns play the same or similar role, which values must stay intact, which text may wrap naturally, and where existing row height could absorb wrapping.
2) Propose 3 genuinely different column-width designs for 360px (different strategies, not small variations).
Reply ONLY JSON: {"understanding":{"purpose":"","reading":"","groups":["columns that belong together and why"],"keep_intact":[""],"may_wrap":[""]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[int px per column, column 1 first],"idea":"one sentence"}]}

log.raw: {"understanding":{"purpose":"Compare checkout outcomes between control and variant, including effect size and statistical evidence across seven metrics.","reading":"Readers scan metric names down the first column, compare each control mean with its variant mean and confidence intervals, then check lift and p-value. Each row should remain easy to follow across the table.","groups":["Control mean and 95% CI belong together, as do variant mean and 95% CI; corresponding control and variant columns should have comparable widths.","Lift and p-value summarize the difference and its statistical evidence, so they form a related pair."],"keep_intact":["Numeric values, percentages, currency amounts, time values, confidence interval endpoints and p-values should remain intact where possible.","Metric names should remain recognizable, with individual words kept intact where space permits."],"may_wrap":["Metric names can wrap at spaces; longer names can use additional row height.","Confidence intervals may wrap at a range separator if necessary, while keeping each endpoint intact.","Grouped headers can wrap if needed."]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[130,73,134,73,131,73,76],"idea":"Use a wide scrolling table with intact numeric values and confidence intervals, while allowing metric names to wrap naturally."},{"name":"B","widths":[120,71,90,70,90,73,76],"idea":"Use moderate horizontal scrolling, preserving individual values while allowing confidence intervals and longer metric names to wrap."},{"name":"C","widths":[100,39,49,39,49,42,41],"idea":"Fit the entire table in the viewport, accepting frequent word and number splitting and taller rows to avoid horizontal scrolling."}]}
